name: Tara Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Dr Dubois. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, and it's Tara. I work at the Harbour Street Clinic in a seaside town, and in summer the place triples in size with tourists, so half my patients are people with sunburn, jellyfish stings and lost blood-pressure tablets. Normal day is 8 till 6.30, about thirty patients, and twice a week I do an evening shift at the out-of-hours service on top for extra money. I'm one year qualified and I'm still slow at the tricky stuff, like knowing when a tired older person is just tired or actually unwell.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the puzzle part, and I love the fishermen, who never come in until a cut is properly infected and then apologise for wasting my time. What wears me out is admin: the clinic's computer system is about fifteen years old and every letter takes six clicks. I use AI tools every day already, on my own phone, to draft patient leaflets in plain words and to double-check drug doses, though some of the older doctors think that's lazy. Money-wise I'm stretched, with a car loan, a student loan and maybe two weeks' savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that would be a bit of a let-down for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud, probably on my group chat with my old med school friends: told you it wasn't magic, but it's still a decent tool. At work I'd keep nudging the practice manager to let us use a proper approved note-writing tool. I'd say the problems in this town are about too few doctors and too much paperwork, not about whether AI is clever enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd mean nothing changes for me, and nothing changing isn't great. I'm on lower pay, I've got two weeks' savings, and the only other family doctor jobs nearby are forty minutes inland. I was kind of counting on AI to take the admin so I could see more patients and get better faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the two out-of-hours evenings a week, because that's what pays the car loan. I'd keep using AI on my phone for leaflets and dose checks. And from January I'd put the out-of-hours money from one shift a month straight into savings, so maybe £150 a month, until I've got three months put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, mostly. A bit of disappointment, and the usual end-of-month worry when the car loan and rent go out on the same day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some older doctors think using AI is lazy. Has that caused any trouble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dr Hughes, who's been at the clinic for thirty years, once saw a leaflet I'd made and asked who wrote it. I said I did, with help, and he went a bit cold. I get it, he learned everything the hard way, but the leaflet was better than the photocopied one from 2009 with the wrong phone number on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing much changes, where do you see yourself in a couple of years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still at Harbour Street, probably, still doing out-of-hours, with a bit more confidence and a bit less debt. I'd quite like to run the clinic's diabetes work one day, because the town has loads of it and nobody owns it. But I'm not going to get rich, and I'll still check my bank app before I buy anything.

say: I'd say AI was never **magic**, but it's still a decent tool for doctors.
I'd tell the practice manager we need an **approved note tool**, because paperwork is the real problem.
think: Nothing changing isn't great when I'm on **lower pay** with two weeks of savings.
I was counting on AI taking **admin** so I could see more patients and learn faster.
do: Keep doing **two out-of-hours** evenings a week to cover the car loan.
Put one shift's pay, about **£150 a month**, into savings from January.
Keep using AI on my phone for **leaflets** and dose checks.
feel: The usual **end-of-month** worry when rent and the car loan go out together.
S0.quote: I was kind of counting on AI to take the admin so I could see more patients and get better faster.
fieldNote: Unlike most, she'd be **disappointed** by a plateau; she wanted the help.
Her pressures are real anyway: **car loan**, student loan, two weeks' savings.
Already uses AI daily, which puts her at odds with a **senior colleague**.
Has a quiet ambition to own the clinic's **diabetes** work.

steps.text: Keep two out-of-hours evening shifts a week
Save one shift's pay, about £150 a month, from January
Keep making plain-word patient leaflets with AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's the one I've been half expecting. The thinking tasks first, yes, that matches what I see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud and with some excitement: this is our chance to fix the paperwork and get back to patients. I'd also say, just as loudly, that the savings have to go into more appointments, not into someone's profits. I'd probably write a post about it on the doctors' forum I lurk on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm well placed. I'm the person at Harbour Street who already uses this stuff, so I'd be the one showing everyone else how. The risk is that the health authority uses it to hire fewer juniors, and I'm a junior, so I'm not daft about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to run the pilot of an AI scribe at the clinic, the kind that listens to the visit and writes the notes, and ask for an extra session a week paid to do it. I'd join the union's working group on AI, because I'd rather be at the table than shouting from outside. And I'd do an online course on clinical safety for AI tools, the free one from the medical college, in my evenings off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly energised, with a little knot in my stomach. I'm more excited than scared, but I'd be lying if I said the junior job cuts didn't cross my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the clinic would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dr Hughes, actually, the one who thinks I'm lazy. He's sixty-one and he hates the computer, and if the clinic suddenly expects everyone to work with an AI scribe, he'll either retire early or be miserable. I'd want to help him, even if he'd hate being helped by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're excited, but also that juniors might be hired less. Does that worry you more than you're letting on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. My contract runs to next September, and if the health authority decides one AI-assisted doctor can do what two did, I'd be the newest one in the room. That's why I'd make myself the person running the AI pilot at our clinic, so I'm the doctor the clinic can't easily lose.

think: I'm **well placed**, because I already use these tools more than anyone at the clinic.

Join the union's **AI working group** this year.
Do the medical college's free **clinical safety** course for AI tools in the evenings.

fieldNote: She sees **opportunity** first, then the threat to junior posts, and plans around both.
Running the pilot is partly a **job-security** move; she admits it when pressed.
Progressive streak shows in insisting gains go to **patients**, not profits.
Shows real care for an older colleague who **disapproves** of her.

steps.text: Run an AI scribe pilot at Harbour Street for a paid session

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say we need emergency rules, fast: who's responsible when the AI gets a diagnosis wrong, how patients' data is protected, and what happens to staff. I'd be on the forum and probably on the local radio if they asked, saying the gains need to be shared. I'd say the government should take a stake in the companies, not just regulate them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job changes fast and my pay is at risk. If the AI can do the thinking, the clinic only needs doctors to do examinations and to take responsibility, and it'll want the experienced ones for that. I'd have about three years before robots, where the hands-on bit keeps me useful, but I'm not the best at hands-on yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first month, I'd apply for a clinical safety role with whoever is building these systems, because they'll need doctors who understand both sides, and I'd do it part-time alongside the clinic if I could. I'd keep the out-of-hours shifts, because those are hands-on and in person. And I'd sell my car and get a cheaper one, which saves about £120 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but in a way that makes me move rather than freeze. Like a busy night in out-of-hours when everything arrives at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the patients in this town, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fishermen would probably love a phone app that tells them their cut is infected without having to sit in a waiting room. But the older people, the ones on their own in the flats by the harbour, would get lost. I'd worry that the town gets a cheaper health service and calls it progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the technology. I'd blame governments that saw this coming for years and did nothing, and companies that sell to health services with no one checking. I'd also blame us a bit, doctors, for sticking our heads in the sand.

I'd say the government should take a **stake** in the AI companies, not just regulate them.
think: My job changes fast and my **pay** is at risk, since clinics would keep experienced doctors.
I'd get about **three years** before robots, but I'm not strong at hands-on work yet.

fieldNote: Her fear is about **income**, not identity; she'd act within weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I can work with five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get it right if the health authority starts training now. I'd push the union to ask for paid study time for every doctor to learn the new systems. Online I'd share practical things, like which tools are safe and which ones invent things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think five years suits someone like me. I'd finish my family medicine training by 2029, and I'd already be the one who knows the tools. The risk is still money, though: if the health authority squeezes pay while everyone adjusts, two weeks' savings won't carry me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time master's in health informatics, which is basically how data and computers are used in health care, in 2027, paid by the out-of-hours shifts. I'd get properly good at the hands-on side too, joint injections and minor surgery, because that's my buffer until 2034. And I'd get my savings to three months before 2029, whatever it takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy and hopeful, mostly. A bit tired just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for a master's on lower pay and two weeks' savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd have to drop to one out-of-hours shift to find the time, which makes it harder. I'd ask the health authority for study funding, and if they said no, I'd do it slowly over three years. My mum has offered to help before and I always say no, but I might say yes this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of this change where you'd live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If the interesting jobs end up in the city, two hours away, I might have to go. I'd be sad to leave the sea, and the fishermen, but I'm not going to stay in a seaside town with no work just because I like the view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's almost the right speed, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a proper chance to do it fairly: train everyone, protect the people whose jobs go, and make the tools public, not owned by three companies. I'd say that at union meetings and online. I'd say we doctors have no excuse not to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is good for me. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, a fully trained family doctor with a health data qualification, which is exactly the kind of person a clinic would want leading the change. The robots coming in 2039 matter less, because the hands-on part was never going to be my main thing anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the master's slowly, over three years, without burning out. I'd keep using AI every day and keep a record of where it goes wrong, which I could publish. And I'd take a regional role helping clinics set up AI safely, once I'm qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. Hopeful. The money worry doesn't go away, but in ten years it's my own choices that matter, not the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money worry doesn't go away. What would you do about it with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the car loan in two years, then put the out-of-hours money into savings. By 2030 I'd want six months saved, which sounds like nothing to some people but would be the most I've ever had. I'd also stop saying no to my mum's help, which is hard for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger self, starting medical school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the computers as well as the bodies, and don't be embarrassed about it. Some of the doctors who teased me for using AI will be asking me how it works.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd adapt, but my money wouldn't, and the older patients in this town would get left behind. What would help is paid time to retrain, some kind of income guarantee while health workers switch roles, and clear rules on who's responsible when the AI gets it wrong.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether the people building these things have ever sat in a seaside clinic in August. The tools are built in offices for tidy cases, and nothing in my waiting room is tidy. Someone like me should be in the room when they're designed.

With ten years she becomes **calm**, planning to lead AI work in clinics.
